source_sentences.text: The tricarboxylic acid cycle, also termed the Krebs cycle, constitutes the central oxidative pathway of aerobic metabolism and occurs within the mitochondrial matrix.
Acetyl-CoA, derived from the catabolism of carbohydrates, fatty acids and amino acids, condenses with oxaloacetate to yield citrate, a six-carbon tricarboxylic acid.
Through a sequence of isomerisation, decarboxylation and dehydrogenation reactions, citrate is progressively converted back to oxaloacetate, thereby regenerating the acceptor molecule.
Each turn of the cycle liberates 2 CO₂ and generates 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP by substrate-level phosphorylation.
Because one glucose molecule yields two acetyl-CoA, two turns are required per glucose.
The reduced coenzymes NADH and FADH₂ subsequently donate their electrons to the electron transport chain, where oxidative phosphorylation drives the synthesis of the majority of cellular ATP.

Isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are key regulatory enzymes, allosterically inhibited by high ratios of ATP to ADP and NADH to NAD⁺, which couples the flux of the cycle to the energetic demands of the cell.

expert.text: The tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle serves as the central oxidative pathway of aerobic metabolism inside the mitochondrial matrix.
Acetyl-CoA, produced from carbohydrate, fatty acid, and amino acid breakdown, condenses with oxaloacetate to form six-carbon citrate.
A series of isomerisation, decarboxylation, and dehydrogenation reactions gradually convert citrate back into oxaloacetate to regenerate the acceptor molecule.
One turn of the cycle releases 2 CO₂ and yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, and 1 GTP via substrate-level phosphorylation.
Since a single glucose molecule generates two acetyl-CoA molecules, two complete turns are required per glucose.
NADH and FADH₂ transfer their electrons to the electron transport chain, driving oxidative phosphorylation to synthesize most cellular ATP.
Isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase regulate cycle speed through allosteric inhibition by elevated ATP/ADP and NADH/NAD⁺ ratios.

grade10.text: The Krebs cycle is the main oxygen-using pathway for cell energy and takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.
Acetyl-CoA from broken-down fats, sugars, and proteins combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
Citrate goes through multiple chemical changes to reform oxaloacetate so the cycle can start again.
Each turn produces 2 carbon dioxide molecules, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, and 1 GTP molecule.
Because breaking down one glucose gives two acetyl-CoA molecules, the cycle turns twice per glucose.
NADH and FADH₂ carry electrons to the electron transport chain, which generates most of the cell's ATP.
Key enzymes control the cycle's speed and slow down when cell energy levels like ATP and NADH are high.

grade6.text: The Krebs cycle helps cells turn food into usable energy.
This energy cycle happens inside the mitochondria of the cell.
Acetyl-CoA comes from breaking down food like sugars and fats.
Acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetate to form a molecule named citrate.
Citrate changes step by step back into oxaloacetate.
Each turn releases two carbon dioxide molecules into the cell.
Each turn also creates three NADH and one FADH2 molecule.
One GTP molecule forms during each turn of the cycle.
One sugar molecule powers two full turns of the cycle.
NADH and FADH2 help make most of the cell's ATP.
Special control proteins regulate how fast the cycle runs.
High energy levels slow down the entire cycle when needed.

glossary.plain: A series of chemical reactions in cells that burns nutrients to make energy molecules.
The inner space of the mitochondrion where the Krebs cycle takes place.
A small molecule made from digested food that feeds into the Krebs cycle.
The starting and ending molecule of the Krebs cycle that binds acetyl-CoA.
Electron-carrying helper molecules that transport energy to make ATP later.
A direct chemical reaction that makes energy molecules like GTP or ATP.
The process of making ATP using electrons carried to the electron transport chain.
The slowing down of an enzyme when a molecule binds to it and changes its shape.
